title: Iron Hans
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was a king who owned a great forest near his palace, full of every kind of wild animal. One day he sent out a huntsman to shoot a roe deer for him, but the man never came back. “Perhaps something has happened to him,” said the king. The next day he sent out two more huntsmen to look for him, but they stayed away too. On the third day he summoned all his huntsmen and said, “Search the whole forest, and don’t give up until you have found all three.” But none of these came home either, and none was ever seen again. From then on nobody would dare to enter the forest. It lay there in deep stillness and solitude, and nothing could be seen of it except an eagle or a hawk now and then flying over. This went on for many years, until a huntsman nobody knew presented himself to the king, looking for a position, and offered to go into the dangerous forest. The king would not agree. “It isn’t safe in there,” he said. “I’m afraid you would do no better than the others, and you would never come out again.” The huntsman answered, “Sire, I’ll take the risk on myself. I don’t know what fear is.”

So the huntsman went off to the forest with his dog. Before long the dog picked up the scent of some game and wanted to chase it. But it had barely run two steps when it came to a deep pool and could go no farther. A naked arm reached up out of the water, seized the dog, and pulled it under. When the huntsman saw this, he went back and fetched three men with buckets to bail out the water. When they could see the bottom, there lay a wild man whose body was brown like rusty iron, and whose hair hung over his face and down to his knees. They tied him up with ropes and led him away to the castle. Everyone was astonished at the wild man. The king had him put in an iron cage in his courtyard and forbade anyone, on pain of death, to open the door, and the queen herself was to keep the key. From then on, everyone could safely go into the forest again.

The king had a son, eight years old, who was playing in the courtyard one day when his golden ball rolled into the cage. The boy ran over and said, “Give me my ball.” “Not until you open the door for me,” answered the man. “No,” said the boy. “I won’t do that. The king has forbidden it.” And he ran away. The next day he went again and asked for his ball. The wild man said, “Open my door,” but the boy refused. On the third day the king had ridden out to hunt, and the boy went once more and said, “I couldn’t open the door even if I wanted to, because I don’t have the key.” Then the wild man said, “It’s under your mother’s pillow. You can get it from there.” The boy, who wanted his ball back, threw every worry to the wind and brought the key. The door opened stiffly, and the boy pinched his fingers. Once it was open, the wild man stepped out, handed him the golden ball, and hurried off. The boy had grown frightened. He called and cried after him, “Oh, wild man, don’t go away, or I’ll be beaten!” The wild man turned back, picked him up, set him on his shoulder, and strode quickly into the forest. When the king came home, he noticed the empty cage and asked the queen how it had happened. She knew nothing about it and looked for the key, but it was gone. She called the boy, but nobody answered. The king sent people to search for him in the fields, but they didn’t find him. Then it was easy for him to guess what had happened, and great grief settled over the royal court.

When the wild man had reached the dark forest again, he lifted the boy down from his shoulder and said to him, “You will never see your father and mother again, but I’ll keep you with me, because you set me free and I feel pity for you. If you do everything I tell you, you’ll be well off. I have more treasure and gold than anyone in the world.” He made a bed of moss for the boy to sleep on. The next morning the man took him to a well and said, “Look, the golden well is as bright and clear as crystal. You are to sit beside it and make sure that nothing falls in, or it will be spoiled. I’ll come every evening to see whether you have obeyed my order.” The boy sat down at the edge of the well. Often he saw a golden fish or a golden snake appear in it, and he took care that nothing fell in. While he was sitting there, his finger began to hurt so badly that without meaning to he put it in the water. He pulled it out again quickly, but saw that it was completely gilded, and however hard he tried to wash the gold off, it was no use. In the evening Iron Hans came back, looked at the boy, and said, “What has happened to the well?” “Nothing, nothing,” he answered, and held his finger behind his back so the man wouldn’t see it. But Iron Hans said, “You dipped your finger in the water. This time I’ll let it pass, but make sure you never let anything fall in again.” At daybreak the boy was already sitting by the well, keeping watch. His finger hurt again, and he ran it over his head, and sadly, a hair fell into the well. He snatched it out quickly, but it was already completely gilded. Iron Hans came and knew right away what had happened. “You let a hair fall into the well,” he said. “I’ll allow you to watch over it one more time, but if it happens a third time, the well is spoiled and you can’t stay with me any longer.”

On the third day the boy sat by the well and didn’t move his finger, however much it hurt. But time dragged for him, and he looked at the reflection of his face on the surface of the water. As he leaned down further and further, trying to look straight into his own eyes, his long hair slid from his shoulders into the water. He straightened up quickly, but all the hair on his head had already turned to gold and shone like the sun. You can imagine how terrified the poor boy was! He took out his handkerchief and tied it around his head so the man wouldn’t see. When Iron Hans came, he already knew everything and said, “Take off the handkerchief.” Then the golden hair streamed out, and no matter how the boy tried to make excuses, it was useless. “You have failed the test and cannot stay here any longer. Go out into the world, and there you’ll learn what poverty is. But since you don’t have a bad heart, and since I mean well by you, there is one thing I’ll grant you. If you ever get into trouble, come to the forest and cry out ‘Iron Hans,’ and I will come and help you. My power is great, greater than you think, and I have gold and silver in plenty.”

Then the king’s son left the forest and walked on and on, over beaten paths and unbeaten ones, until at last he came to a great city. He looked for work there but found none, and he had learned nothing that could help him get by. In the end he went to the palace and asked whether they would take him in. The people at court had no idea what use they could make of him, but they liked him and told him to stay. Eventually the cook hired him and said he could carry wood and water and rake the cinders together. Once, when nobody else happened to be around, the cook ordered him to carry the food to the royal table. But because he didn’t want his golden hair to be seen, he kept his little cap on. Nothing like that had ever happened before in the king’s presence, and the king said, “When you come to the royal table, you must take your hat off.” He answered, “Ah, Sire, I can’t. I have a bad sore on my head.” Then the king had the cook summoned, scolded him, and asked how he could have taken on such a boy, and told him to send the boy away at once. The cook, however, felt sorry for him and swapped him for the gardener’s boy.

From then on the boy had to plant and water the garden, hoe and dig, and put up with the wind and every kind of weather. One summer day, when he was working alone out there, it was so hot that he took off his little cap to let the air cool his head. The sun struck his hair and made it glitter and flash, and the light reached into the king’s daughter’s bedroom. She jumped up to see what it was. She spotted the boy and called down to him, “Boy, bring me a wreath of flowers!” He pulled his cap back on as fast as he could, picked some wild flowers from the fields, and tied them together. As he was climbing the stairs with them, the gardener stopped him and said, “How can you bring the king’s daughter a garland of such ordinary flowers? Go back at once and get others. Look for the prettiest and the rarest.” “Oh, no,” the boy answered, “the wild ones smell sweeter, and she will like them better.” When he came into the room, the king’s daughter said, “Take off your cap. It isn’t proper to keep it on in front of me.” Again he said, “I can’t. My head is sore.” But she grabbed his cap and pulled it off, and his golden hair tumbled down over his shoulders, a wonderful sight. He tried to run out, but she held him by the arm and pressed a handful of ducats on him. He left with them, but he cared nothing for the gold. He took the coins to the gardener and said, “These are for your children. They can play with them.” The next day the king’s daughter called to him again and told him to bring her a wreath of field flowers. When he went in with it, she snatched at his cap at once and tried to take it from him, but he held on to it with both hands. Again she gave him a handful of ducats, and again he wouldn’t keep them, but gave them to the gardener as toys for his children. On the third day it all went the same way. She couldn’t get the cap off his head, and he wouldn’t take her money.

Not long after that, war broke out and the country was invaded. The king called his people together. He didn’t know whether he could stand against the enemy, who were stronger and had a mighty army. Then the gardener’s boy said, “I’m grown now, and I want to go to war too. Just give me a horse.” The others laughed and said, “Find one for yourself once we’re gone. We’ll leave one behind for you in the stable.” After they had marched off, he went to the stable and led the horse out. It was lame in one leg and went hobblety jib, hobblety jib, but he climbed on anyway and rode off toward the dark forest. At the edge of the trees he called “Iron Hans!” three times, so loudly that it rang through the woods. The wild man appeared at once and said, “What do you want?” “I need a strong horse, because I’m going to the war.” “You shall have it, and more than you ask.” Then the wild man went back into the forest. Before long a stable-boy came out leading a horse that snorted through its nostrils and could barely be held back. Behind them came a great troop of warriors, dressed from head to foot in iron, their swords flashing in the sun. The young man handed his three-legged horse over to the stable-boy, mounted the other, and rode at the head of the soldiers. By the time he neared the battlefield, a great many of the king’s men had already fallen, and the rest were close to giving way. The young man galloped in with his iron soldiers, swept over the enemy like a hurricane, and cut down everyone who stood against him. The enemy began to run, but he chased them and never stopped until not a single man was left. Instead of going back to the king, though, he led his troop along side paths to the forest and called out for Iron Hans. “What do you want?” asked the wild man. “Take back your horse and your soldiers, and give me my three-legged horse again.” Everything he asked for was done, and soon he was riding along on his three-legged horse. When the king came home to his palace, his daughter went out to meet him and congratulated him on his victory. “I’m not the one who won it,” he said. “A strange knight came to my aid with his soldiers.” The daughter wanted to know who the strange knight was, but the king couldn’t tell her. “He went after the enemy,” he said, “and I never saw him again.” She asked the gardener where his boy was. He smiled and said, “He’s just got home on his three-legged horse, and the others have been jeering at him and shouting, ‘Here comes our hobblety jib back again!’ They asked him, too, ‘What hedge were you sleeping under all this time?’ And he said, ‘I did the best of anyone, and things would have gone badly without me.’ That only made them laugh at him more.”

The king said to his daughter, “I’ll announce a great feast that will last three days, and you will throw a golden apple. Maybe the unknown man will show himself.” When the feast was proclaimed, the young man went out to the forest and called for Iron Hans. “What do you want?” asked the wild man. “I want to catch the king’s daughter’s golden apple.” “Consider it yours already,” said Iron Hans. “You’ll also have a suit of red armor for the day, and a spirited chestnut horse to ride.” When the day came, the young man galloped to the field and took his place among the knights, and no one recognized him. The king’s daughter stepped forward and threw a golden apple to the knights. None of them caught it except him, and the moment he had it he galloped away.

On the second day Iron Hans dressed him as a white knight and gave him a white horse. Once more he was the only one to catch the apple, and he didn’t stay a moment, but galloped off with it. The king became angry. “This is not allowed,” he said. “He must come before me and tell me his name.” He ordered that if the knight who caught the apple rode away again, they were to go after him, and if he refused to come back willingly, they were to cut him down and stab him.

On the third day Iron Hans gave him a suit of black armor and a black horse, and once more he caught the apple. But as he rode away with it, the king’s attendants chased him, and one of them came so close that the point of his sword wounded the young man in the leg. Still, he got away from them. But his horse bucked so wildly that the helmet fell off his head, and they saw that he had golden hair. They rode back and told the king.

The next day the king’s daughter asked the gardener about his boy. “He’s out working in the garden. That odd fellow went to the festival too, and only came home last evening. He’s even shown my children three golden apples that he won.”

The king had him called in, and he came with his little cap on his head again. But the king’s daughter went up to him and took it off, and his golden hair fell down over his shoulders. He was so handsome that everyone was amazed. “Are you the knight who came to the festival every day, always in different colors, and caught the three golden apples?” asked the king. “Yes,” he answered, “and here are the apples.” He took them out of his pocket and gave them back to the king. “If you want more proof, you can see the wound your men gave me when they chased me. And I am also the knight who helped you win the victory over your enemies.” “If you can do deeds like that, you are no gardener’s boy. Tell me, who is your father?” “My father is a mighty king, and I have as much gold as I could ever need.” “I can see that I owe you my thanks,” said the king. “Is there anything I can do to please you?” “Yes,” he answered, “there is. Give me your daughter for my wife.” The young woman laughed and said, “He doesn’t stand on ceremony, does he? But I had already seen from his golden hair that he was no gardener’s boy.” Then she went and kissed him. His father and mother came to the wedding and were overjoyed, for they had given up all hope of ever seeing their dear son again. And as they sat at the wedding feast, the music suddenly stopped, the doors opened, and a stately king walked in with a great retinue. He went up to the young man, embraced him, and said, “I am Iron Hans. I was turned into a wild man by enchantment, but you have set me free. All the treasures I own shall be yours.”
